title: Frontend Architecture: Module Boundaries and Refactoring
description: Design dependency direction, assign state ownership, refactor duplicated behavior and make errors recoverable.
learningOutcomes: Define module boundaries around responsibilities and reasons to change.
Explain import direction and recognize circular dependencies.
Assign URL, server, shared and local UI state to suitable owners.
Refactor duplication behind a stable contract without building unnecessary abstractions.
Design consistent error states and repeatable verification.

blocks.text: Architecture is the shape of change

A useful architecture helps a developer find the behavior they need to change, understand which layer owns it, and verify the result. A module should have a coherent responsibility and a clear public interface. Folder names alone do not create architecture: dependency direction, data ownership and testing boundaries matter more than whether a project uses a particular folder template.

blocks.code:
Route / page
  -> Feature orchestration
      -> Custom Hook / state transition
          -> Service / API contract
      -> UI components (props in, callbacks out)
Shared primitives and tokens <- feature UI

Avoid these reverse edges:
UI primitive -> route page
Service -> React component
Feature A <-> Feature B circular imports

steps.title: Keep orchestration close to a user journey
steps.explanation: The route composes a feature and the feature coordinates the workflow. A custom Hook can own reusable lifecycle/state behavior without turning every function into a Hook.

steps.title: Keep service and presentation contracts separate
steps.explanation: A service knows the transport/data contract; a UI component renders values and emits events. Components do not need to know HTTP details, and the service does not need to import JSX.

steps.title: Shared dependencies should stay lower-level
steps.explanation: UI primitives can be consumed by features, but importing route pages back into a primitive creates a reverse dependency. Mutual imports between features make changes and tests harder to isolate.

items: Group files by a feature when they change together; group by technical type when the application is small and the shared layer is still clear. Neither convention is universal.
A module boundary should reflect a reason to change, a stable contract, or an independently testable responsibility—not simply a file count.
Keep URL state for shareable/filterable navigation, server state near its data-fetching/cache boundary, and transient interaction state local unless multiple consumers need a shared owner.
Refactor in small steps: characterize current behavior with tests, introduce a seam, move one responsibility, run checks, then remove duplication.
An error boundary catches rendering failures, while request errors and form errors need their own explicit states. One generic try/catch is not an error strategy for every layer.

blocks.prompt: Which dependency direction best fits a reusable Button component in a layered frontend application?

options.text: The Button imports the route page to know when it should render
options.feedback: A low-level UI primitive should not depend on an application route. The page should compose the Button.

options.text: Feature UI imports the shared Button and passes props/callbacks
options.feedback: This keeps the shared primitive lower-level and lets the feature own the user journey.

options.text: The API service imports Button and displays HTTP errors directly
options.feedback: A service should return a clear result/error contract; presentation belongs to the UI layer.

options.text: Two features import each other to share state implicitly
options.feedback: Mutual imports create circular dependencies and obscure state ownership.

blocks.explanation: Dependency direction should make lower-level modules reusable and keep responsibilities explicit.

blocks.title: Refactor a tightly coupled feature into clear boundaries
blocks.context: Given a page that fetches data, validates responses, renders forms and shares helper logic through circular imports, propose and implement a safer boundary.
instructions: Draw the current dependency graph and mark any circular imports.
Move HTTP/status parsing into a service contract and map its outcomes into explicit UI states.
Choose owners for URL filters, server data and transient modal state.
Extract one repeated UI behavior behind a small reusable contract, keeping the feature-specific decisions in the feature.
Define tests that protect current behavior before and after the refactor.
requirements: The dependency graph has a clear direction and no feature-to-feature cycle.
HTTP concerns and presentation concerns have separate interfaces.
State ownership matches sharing and persistence requirements.
The abstraction is justified by reuse or a stable contract, not created only to reduce line count.
Tests cover success, empty and error/recovery behavior.
hints: Start by identifying which layer has the authority to decide each behavior.
If a value should survive refresh and be shared by link, consider URL state.
Refactor one seam at a time so a failing test localizes the change.
successCriteria: A target dependency graph is documented.
State owners and layer interfaces are explicit.
Circular imports are removed or justified with a better boundary.
Behavior-preserving and failure-state tests are listed.

items: Architecture helps locate change and verify behavior; folder layout alone does not create it.
Keep dependency direction deliberate and state ownership explicit.
Refactor in small, testable steps and distinguish rendering, request and validation errors.
